passage: Two days after the outage, the team gathered in the small meeting room at the Hyderabad office with a whiteboard. Pankaj, who had pushed the release, sat with his arms crossed. Baljeet, leading the review, began, 'We're here to ask what let this happen, not who.' They built the timeline first: the deploy at 6:10, the first errors at 6:25, the customer report at 7:05. Then the causes. No alert had fired for the failing payments, and the rollback had never been tested, so it took forty minutes to work out. Pankaj uncrossed his arms and said, 'I should have tested it too,' and Baljeet answered, 'Then let's make the test part of every release.' Each action got an owner and a date: an alert, a rollback test, a checklist. The blame column stayed empty.

qa.q: Which two causes did the team find?
qa.a: No alert had fired for the failing payments, and the rollback had never been tested.

qa.q: What do Pankaj's crossed arms suggest at the start of the meeting?
qa.a: Pankaj was probably defensive and afraid of being blamed, and he relaxed once the review focused on the system.

qa.q: What could the team do to make sure the actions get finished?
qa.a: They could check the action list at the next team meeting, since owners and dates only help if someone looks at them again.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team have felt hearing 'what let this happen, not who'?
qa.a: They were probably relieved and more willing to speak honestly, since nobody had to fear punishment.

grounding: Shows a team writing a timeline, naming the missing alert and untested rollback as causes and assigning owned actions without blaming a person.

passage:
Hi Rashmi,
You asked for a summary of last week's postmortem, since you joined after the outage. Here it is, short.
Timeline: 14:02 bad release; 14:40 first customer complaint; 15:10 we noticed; 15:25 rollback attempted and failed; 16:30 service restored by hand.
Root causes, not people: the alert for checkout errors had been switched off during a test in March and never turned back on. And our rollback script had never been tested on the new servers.
Actions, each with an owner and a date: alert audit, Farhan, 30 June. Monthly rollback test, Keerthana, first one 5 July. Release checklist to include 'alerts on?', me, this week.
Nobody was named as the cause. The engineer who made the release sat in the room and helped write the timeline. That's how we want it.
Jyoti

qa.a: The rollback script had never been tested on the new servers.

qa.q: How might the engineer who made the release have felt in that room?
qa.a: The engineer probably arrived anxious and ashamed, then felt relieved to help write the timeline instead of being blamed.

qa.q: What could Rashmi do as the new manager to keep this approach going?
qa.a: Rashmi could follow up on each owner's date and share progress openly, so actions don't quietly lapse.

qa.q: How does this postmortem look to Rashmi, who joined after the outage?
qa.a: Rashmi gets a clear, blame-free picture of what happened and what is changing, which makes the team's process easier to trust.

grounding: It shows a team writing a timeline, finding root causes in a missing alert and an untested rollback, and listing actions with owners rather than punishing anyone.

passage: Ramesh, you asked what a blameless postmortem actually is. Let me tell you about ours. I'm Arohi, and I ran it. Two weeks ago our app was down for three hours. In the room, everyone was looking at Karan, who'd pushed the release. I said, before anything else, 'We're here to fix the system, not to find a villain.' Then we built the timeline on the whiteboard, minute by minute. And the real problems appeared: the alert that should have woken someone had been muted months ago, and our rollback had never been tested. That's why three hours, not fifteen minutes. We wrote four actions, each with a name and a date. Karan took one himself, testing rollback monthly. He told me afterwards it was the first time he didn't want to hide after a mistake.

qa.q: How long was the app down?
How did Karan feel after the postmortem?
qa.a: Karan felt safe for once, relieved not to want to hide after a mistake.

qa.q: What else could Arohi do to make sure the four actions happen?
qa.a: Arohi could check each action at the next team meeting and close the postmortem only when all four are done.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team see the opening line about no villain?
qa.a: It likely eased their tension, letting them look at the system honestly instead of watching Karan.

grounding: It shows a postmortem building a timeline, finding root causes in a muted alert and an untested rollback, and assigning owned actions rather than blame.
